extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students/researchers of manga, and creators of shōjo manga
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for creating shōjo manga — the visual, narrative, thematic, publication, and marketing conventions associated with manga aimed at adolescent girls and young adult women. Useful for authors, artists, and scholars seeking the genre's characteristic techniques and production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target demographic / editorial category
rubrics_metrics.description: Shōjo manga is an editorial category of Japanese comics targeting an audience of adolescent girls and young adult women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a demographic designation rather than a strict stylistic or genre boundary; works labelled shōjo may vary widely in style and are also read by men and older women. When producing or evaluating shōjo manga, consider intended readership (age/gender) and market placement (dedicated shōjo magazines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication format and serialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Shōjo manga is traditionally published in dedicated manga magazines, serialized before being collected as books and collected volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan pacing and chapter breaks for serialization; expect editorial feedback and reader polls to influence plotting. Serialization strategy influences story length, cliffhangers, and episodic hooks; collected volumes may allow different presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on human relations and emotions (ningen kankei)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invariant characteristic of shōjo manga has been a focus on human relations and the emotions that accompany them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives typically foreground interpersonal relationships (friendship, affection, love) and interior emotional experience rather than external action; conflicts are frequently resolved through dialogue and emotional exchange rather than physical combat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on interiority and inner monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Shōjo shōsetsu–influenced narration emphasizes the inner monologue of the protagonist and 'flowery and emotional' prose style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express internal feelings visually and textually (thought captions, asides, punctuation). Use techniques such as ellipses, exclamation points, and dashes to convey fragmented or heightened emotion; allow sequences that slow down to explore inner states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-verbal visual elements to convey feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration is often punctuated with non-verbal elements that express the feelings of the protagonists (e.g., flowers, ribbons, fluttering dresses, words that string across the page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate decorative motifs and background symbolism (flowers, sparkles, ribbons) and integrate onomatopoeia and floating text across the page to externalize emotion and mood; these devices help communicate tone and affect without explicit dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel layout conventions (naihō / kaihō / mahaku)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three major aspects of panel construction distinguish shōjo manga: naiho ('panel encapsulations' — breaking or removing panel borders), kaiho ('release' — decompression and languid sequences), and mahaku ('break' — symbolic use of white space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overlapping or borderless panels, extend elements beyond panel borders, employ decompressed pacing with repeated or angled perspectives, and utilize white space symbolically to slow scenes or emphasize emotion. Remove speech balloons at times and spread text across the page for internal monologue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompression (kaihō) and tempo control
rubrics_metrics.description: Kaihō refers to the use of decompression to create more languid and relaxed sequences; text may be removed from speech balloons and spread across the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow scenes to breathe: linger on emotion, repeat moments from different angles, and use extended visual sequences with minimal dialog to heighten mood. This affects serialization pacing and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic use of white space (mahaku)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mahaku refers to the symbolic use of white space in composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ expansive white areas to isolate characters, create emotional pauses, or signal transitions; white space can function as a visual metaphor for feelings like emptiness or transcendence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large, highly detailed eyes (dekame) and facial close-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: A defining stylistic element is depiction of characters with very large, detailed eyes that have star-shaped highlights; panels often frame close-ups of faces to show emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design eyes with highlights, concentric shading, sparkles, stars, or dot/iris variations to convey nuanced emotion. Use frequent close-ups on faces and eyes as primary emotive devices and gender markers (female characters often drawn with larger eyes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flowery/lyrical painter influence (jojōga) and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Shōjo manga was influenced by jojōga (lyrical painting), characterized by sentimental style, beautiful/fashionable figures, and strong atmosphere focused on emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt decorative illustration approaches, soft lines, fashion-conscious character design, and atmospheric backgrounds. Prioritize mood and aesthetic beauty as part of storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressive typography and onomatopoeia (hirahira)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics point to imaginative use of words that string across the page (onomatopoeia and expressive lettering described by the onomatopoeia 'hirahira').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate hand-lettered effects, floating text, and stylized onomatopoeia to convey emotional texture; place words as graphic elements interacting with art to enhance feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative focus: dialogue and conversation over physical conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: When conflict occurs, the most common medium of exchange is dialogue and conversation, as opposed to physical combat typical in shōnen manga.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on verbal confrontations, misunderstandings, emotional confrontations, and conversations to drive plot and character development rather than action sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themes: gender, sexuality, and role-defying characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that defy traditional roles and stereotypes surrounding gender and sexuality (tomboy protagonists, cross-dressing, androgynous characters) are central motifs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore gender performance, role reversals, and identity through character arcs; use established archetypes (otenba, fighting girl, cross-dressing girl) and consider how such portrayals engage with social change and feminist themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre conventions — yaoi / boys' love
rubrics_metrics.description: Male-male romance manga (yaoi / boys' love) is a significant shōjo subgenre, typically focusing on androgynous men (bishōnen) and romantic fantasy rather than realist depictions of gay relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing BL, emphasize romanticized, idealized relationships, androgyny, and fantasy elements; be aware of scholarly critiques (e.g., distancing female sexuality) and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre conventions — yuri (female-female romance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Female-female romance manga (yuri) has historical links to shōjo; many yuri stories have a 'tragic' bent and often center on romantic friendships dating to Class S works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing yuri within shōjo traditions, consider motifs of intense friendship, emotional intensity, and the historical tendency toward doomed or tragic narratives; be attentive to evolving representations and audience needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror motifs and supernatural themes in shōjo
rubrics_metrics.description: Horror shōjo manga often features supernatural subjects (yūrei, yōkai), urban legends, curses often tied to murdered/harassed women, and resolutions that involve showing compassion for ghosts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use emotionally driven supernatural stories where empathy, guilt, or social critique resolves the haunting. Note that kashi-hon horror could be gorier; mainstream shōjo horror may emphasize psychological and emotional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fashion and costume as narrative/visual element
rubrics_metrics.description: Shōjo manga has a long relationship with fashion: characters often appear in elaborate outfits (ribbons, frills), with inspirations from Victorian fashion, ballet, and era-specific trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clothing to signal character, era, mood, and aspirational identity; when targeting cosplay or merchandise, design iconic outfits. Fashion trends in the manga should reflect the period and readership's taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age and protagonist focus: adolescent vs adult (shōjo vs josei)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shōjo is distinguished primarily by focus on adolescent protagonists and teen readership; josei (ladies' comics) targets adult women and centers adult protagonists though aesthetics may overlap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match protagonist age, themes, and degree of sexual explicitness to the intended demographic; blur boundaries carefully when aiming for cross-demographic appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexuality depiction and censorship navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Depictions of sexuality in shōjo evolved over time; early sex scenes used visual censorship workarounds (e.g., bed sheets) and later genres such as 'teens' love' emerged with more explicit content aimed at older teens/young adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of legal/ethical boundaries and magazine editorial standards. Use framing, implication, and audience-appropriate explicitness when depicting sexuality; different publishers and magazines have varying tolerance levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing, reader feedback, and community-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines foster a sense of community via reader polls, letters (sometimes published), contests, novelty items in issues, coupons/mail-order prizes, and meetings between readers and authors; publishers use polls/letters to change plotlines and decide adaptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage readers via interactive features, solicit and monitor polls and letters, and design hook points that invite feedback. Consider merchandising and bonus items as part of a publication strategy that sustains serialized readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent development through reader submissions/contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines discover new authors through contests in which readers submit manga; many professional artists began via these contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If launching or staffing a shōjo magazine, run submission contests and nurture amateur talent. For creators, produce short, contest-ready one-shots that highlight voice and fit magazine demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-media potential and adaptation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful shōjo manga are often adapted into anime, films, TV dramas, video games, and music CDs; cross-media marketing (publishing across multiple mediums) became prominent in the 2000s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characters, world, and story beats with transmedia adaptation in mind (memorable visuals, strong central relationships, merchandising-friendly elements). Coordinate with publishers on rights and adaptation pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual aesthetic integration for 'moe' and boys' audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: From the 2000s some shōjo magazines targeted anime and boys' love fans by publishing manga that resembled anime visuals, featured bishōnen in fantastical settings, and integrated 'moe' aesthetics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming at these sub-audiences, adapt visual language (moe-style features, bishōnen design), and consider tonality and genre blending to appeal to cross-over readerships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align themes with era and social context
rubrics_metrics.description: Shōjo manga content has evolved in tandem with social change (e.g., family dramas popular in the 1960s; romantic relationships in the 1970s; self-fulfillment and community-protecting heroines in the 1990s), reflecting changing roles of women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextualize themes to contemporary social concerns and reader aspirations: choose whether to evoke nostalgia or address current issues (identity, self-fulfillment, community). Historical awareness informs authenticity and reception.
